newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST-Iberian bond seen outperforming next week.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Iberian bond seen outperforming next week.

text.p: Iberian bonds could once again be a fashionable asset next week, buoyed by positive inflation expectations in the Spanish and Portuguese markets with the short end set to benefit most.

But while Spanish bonds are likely to outperform other markets, long term bonds could still fall, weighed down by the U.S. Treasury blues which could worsen after March payrolls data due later on Friday.

"Given the high sensitivity to U.S. movement, U.S. jobs data will weigh heavily on the market. But the Spanish market is proving healthier than others, and the peseta is also stronger," said Valentin Fernandez chief economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
Analysts expect an increase in the March U.S. jobs figure of around 196,000 versus 339,000 in February, with the unemployment rate falling to 5.2 percent from 5.3 in February.

"We don't expect a market friendly figure today, so it's likely the market will be shaken again by the prospect of further rate hikes in the coming months," said Nuno Godinho, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Lisbon.
"On that basis it's likely the Iberian market will outperform others next week," he added.
Godinho said the 10-year cash spread over Bunds could fall below 100 basis points for Portuguese bonds and to around 110 bps for Spanish bonos.

Spreads were trading on Friday morning at around 106 bps and 116 respectively, lower than the beginning of March when they were around 135 and 145 bps, but still higher than the lows of 80 and 83 seen at the end of January.
The best performing part of the two markets should be the short end, analysts agreed.
"The short end, between two- and three-years, with yields higher than six percent and a positive carry versus the short term rate, could be the best buy right now," said Fernandez.
After Spain's February PPI came in tamer than expected, falling 0.1 percent in the month to a 0.5 percent year-on-year, analysts have become more optimistic about the economy's inflation perspective.
Henrik Lumholdt, economist at Bank of America in Madrid, said March CPI, due on April 11, could come in as low as 2.3/2.4 percent year-on-year after 2.5 percent in February.
Together with the newfound strength in the peseta, the Bank of Spain may see room for another rate cut this month.

"Given the rebounding peseta, and the possible decline in the inflation rate we could expect the Bank of Spain to cut its key money market rate on April 15, and markets are not yet discounting such a move," Lumholdt said.
"The market is not discunting any fall in the official rate before year-end. That's too pessimistic," he added.
A similar scenario is seen in Portugal.

"March inflation data could be a positive surprise, and the Bank of Portugal, whose key money market rate stands at 6.50 percent or 75 basis points higher than Spain's, could start cutting rates," said Godinho.
